Joins without surprises

Source: vignettes/articles/joins.Rmd
joins.Rmd
library(zutable)

A join that runs is not always the join you meant. A key repeated in the lookup table multiplies rows, a missing key matches or not depending on the tool, and an integer key against a double one may match by value or not at all. This article shows what join() does in each case, and how to ask for something else. It assumes you have read vignette("zutable").

We use two small tables throughout. people has a repeated customer, 20, and a row whose key is missing.

orders <- zutable(order = 1:5, customer = c(10L, 20L, 10L, NA, 30L))
people <- zutable(
  customer = c(10L, 20L, 20L, NA),
  name     = c("Ada", "Linus", "Grace", "Nobody")
)

Rows come in a fixed order

An inner join keeps each pair of matching rows. The pairs come in the order of x’s rows, and within one row of x in the order of y’s, so the result reads like orders with names attached.

join(orders, people, on = customer)
#> <zutable> 5 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer name
#>   <int32> <int32>  <string>
#> 1 1       10       Ada
#> 2 2       20       Linus
#> 3 2       20       Grace
#> 4 3       10       Ada
#> 5 4       NA       Nobody

Order 2 appears twice, because customer 20 is in people twice. Order 5 is gone: no person has customer 30.

A repeated key: choose with multiple

multiple says what a row of x gets when it matches several rows of y. The default, "all", gives every pair, as merge() and data.table do. "first" and "last" keep one match, in y’s order.

join(orders, people, on = customer, multiple = "first")
#> <zutable> 4 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer name
#>   <int32> <int32>  <string>
#> 1 1       10       Ada
#> 2 2       20       Linus
#> 3 3       10       Ada
#> 4 4       NA       Nobody
join(orders, people, on = customer, multiple = "last")
#> <zutable> 4 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer name
#>   <int32> <int32>  <string>
#> 1 1       10       Ada
#> 2 2       20       Grace
#> 3 3       10       Ada
#> 4 4       NA       Nobody

When a repeated key means the data is wrong, say so, and the join stops at the first row that fans out:

join(orders, people, on = customer, multiple = "error")
#> Error in `join()`:
#> ! row 2 of x matches 2 rows of y on key (20); multiple = "error"

The error is a zutable_multiple_error, and it names the row and the key.

A missing key: choose with na_equal

By default a missing key matches a missing key, as match() and data.table have it: order 4 found “Nobody” above. SQL has NULL match nothing, and na_equal = FALSE gives SQL’s behaviour.

join(orders, people, on = customer, na_equal = FALSE)
#> <zutable> 4 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer name
#>   <int32> <int32>  <string>
#> 1 1       10       Ada
#> 2 2       20       Linus
#> 3 2       20       Grace
#> 4 3       10       Ada

Keys must have the same type

A key’s type is part of the schema, and the two sides must agree. An integer key against a double one is an error, not a match by value that could silently go wrong on 10.5.

rates <- zutable(customer = c(10, 20), rate = c(0.1, 0.2))
join(orders, rates, on = customer)
#> Error in `join()`:
#> ! key `customer` is int32 in x and `customer` is float64 in y; the types must be the same

Convert one side with cast() first, so the conversion is visible where it happens:

rates_int <- rates[select = .(customer = cast(customer, "int32"), rate)]
join(orders, rates_int, on = customer)
#> <zutable> 3 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer rate
#>   <int32> <int32>  <float64>
#> 1 1       10       0.1
#> 2 2       20       0.2
#> 3 3       10       0.1

Keys with different names are paired with ==, as in on = .(customer == customer_id).

Clashing column names: give suffix

A column that is not a key and is in both tables would be ambiguous in the result, so join() refuses it unless you give the two suffixes.

returns <- zutable(customer = c(10L, 20L), order = 7:8)
join(orders, returns, on = customer)
#> Error in `join()`:
#> ! both tables have a column `order` that is not a key; give `suffix`, as in suffix = c(".x", ".y")
join(orders, returns, on = customer, suffix = c(".x", ".y"))
#> <zutable> 3 rows x 3 columns
#>   order.x customer order.y
#>   <int32> <int32>  <int32>
#> 1 1       10       7
#> 2 2       20       8
#> 3 3       10       7

Which rows to keep: how

how picks the rows. "left" keeps every row of x, "right" every row of y, "full" both. "semi" keeps the rows of x that have a match, once each and with x’s columns only, and "anti" the rows that have none.

join(orders, people, on = customer, how = "full")
#> <zutable> 6 rows x 3 columns
#>   order   customer name
#>   <int32> <int32>  <string>
#> 1 1       10       Ada
#> 2 2       20       Linus
#> 3 2       20       Grace
#> 4 3       10       Ada
#> 5 4       NA       Nobody
#> 6 5       30       NA
join(orders, people, on = customer, how = "semi")
#> <zutable> 4 rows x 2 columns
#>   order   customer
#>   <int32> <int32>
#> 1 1       10
#> 2 2       20
#> 3 3       10
#> 4 4       NA
join(orders, people, on = customer, how = "anti")
#> <zutable> 1 row x 2 columns
#>   order   customer
#>   <int32> <int32>
#> 1 5       30

"semi" keeps order 2 once, although it matches two people, which makes it the safe way to filter by another table.

The index pairs underneath

join() runs on the kernel’s grp_join(), which works on plain vectors and returns the matching row numbers instead of a table. It follows the same rules: x’s order, then y’s, and a missing key matching a missing key.

grp_join(c(10L, 20L, 10L, NA), c(10L, 20L, 20L, NA))
#> $x
#> [1] 1 2 2 3 4
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 1 2 3 1 4

grp_match() is its single-index form, and agrees with match():

x <- c(10L, 20L, 10L, NA, 30L)
y <- c(10L, 20L, 20L, NA)
identical(grp_match(x, y), match(x, y))
#> [1] TRUE

Unlike match(), it takes several key columns at once, as a list or a data frame, without pasting them into one string. Here the rows of x are the pairs (1, 1), (2, 1) and (3, 2), and y holds (2, 1) and (3, 2):

grp_match(list(1:3, c(1L, 1L, 2L)), list(2:3, 1:2))
#> [1] NA  1  2
